Text is accepted in any form for

From: S. Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS



Dear Brian,

I think I've found an applicat-
ion for that seemingly redundant
VAL$ -or maybe I've rediscovered
the wheel?

10 LET a = 10 : LET a$ = "hello"

20 LET b$ = "a$ AND A = 10"
        : REM AND is the keyword

30 PRINT VAL$ b$


This  results in a$ being
printed only if a = 10.


In OUTLETTERS 112 (Dec 1996), in
your reply to Dave Knott about
matters Multiface, you mention
that all the info had been trac-
ed using Francis Miles' index.
Which index is this please, as I
have no memory of seeing this
mentioned.

            Thanks,

        Malcolm Goodman

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

It's still hard to think of a
real application for VAL$. Your
routine could be duplicated with
PRINT a$ AND a = 10 though at
least one can vary a$.

Most computer BASICs seem to use
arrays having variable length
strings for each element instead
of the fixed length that Spectr-
um elements have. One might sim-
ulate that for a few elements up
to 26...

10 RESTORE:READ A$,B$,C$, etc...
20 FOR N = 1 TO 26
30 PRINT VAL$(CHR$(N+64)+"$")
40 NEXT N
50 DATA "one","two","three",etc


Francis Miles index is INDEX
WRITER in OUTLET 92. Run it and
press I then enter outl44-84 to
load and display. It is rather
unwieldy on-screen and it's much
better to print it out.

However, there seem to be some
later data files and I can't see
that they hav been published. My
records seem a bit confused. I
can find a reference to a bug or
something in a later version of
the program but the later data
should be OK. Anyway, it cannot
hurt to put them in this issue
(DISCIPLE/PLUS D ONLY AS THEY
ARE OPENTYPE) so I will add them
now.They are:
  ind.a-d, ind.e-m, and ind.n-z

                       Brian

      Bernadette Dowsland
26 Elsie Street,  Goole,   East
Yorks,DN14 6DU TEL:01405 768665

From: Vic Bishop, LANCASHIRE

Dear Brian,


           MASTERFILE

I read the correspondence from
and to Arnold Yates (who incid-
entally is a friend of mine) in
OUTLET 111 and also your edit-
orial. I also saved OUTDEX1.63
due to thinking of it as a file
rather than as a program and
then continued in the same way
with OUTDEX64.74.

As a result of your answer to
Arnold I then decided to EXPER-
IMENT (quite rightly one of your
favourite words!).


I will start by saying that like
so many of your subscribers my
knowledge is limited and due to
this I am inclined to accept
your instructions or suggestions
as being 'CAST IN STONE'. I also
find a lot of the programs and
formulae in OUTLET beyond my un-
derstanding which can be frustr-
ating.


This is not intended in any way
to be a criticism - only a
comment: most of the people who
write seem to be regular contri-
butors and I often wonder how
many other subscribers are like
myself struggling a bit; but I
DO TRY. SO! back to the subject
matter EXPERIMENTING...


I have now tried saving OUTDEX
as programmes and files so that
they could be compared and found
a number of interesting points -
there are advantages and disad-
vantages with either system...

A PROGRAM enters MFile fully
loaded by using the disc file
and will include DEXSPEC.D
(after its first loading) but,
when printing, will include a
header on every sheet.

A FILE needs MFile loading then
the file DEXSPEC loading each
time you want a print out. It
then prints 255 lines stops and
feeds one page. So if you switch
the printers switch off and wind
back one page and switch the


printer on again it will print
another 255 lines before you
need to repeat the process - the
big advantage being that you
have a much neater looking print
out.

Both methods will hold all prev-
ious files if you merge when
loading. It would seem to be a
matter of choice If you do al-
ways save as a program when you
want a print out you could
always load then save as a file,
reload, add DEXSPEC.D and get a
neater print out;question being,
how often does one need a print
out? I also found that in both
cases once you get past 100 when
you choose ISSUE you start with
100, 101, 102 etc then finally
64, 65, 66 etc.

One point for other dimwits that
caused me some problems - if you
try to save OUTDEX to the OUTLET
disc instead of MFile  and  get
message DISC WRITE PROTECTED -
don't PANIC - press BREAK and GO
TO 1 and do what you should have
done first time. I used start
again by reloading MFile etc.


            +++++++


I read something recently that I
found  so  amusing  that  I
thought it might be appreciated
by OUTLET subscribers. It was an
article in CONNECT, a supplement
in the Daily Telegraph,of a true
story which went as follows:-


The American astronauts were
having severe problems in writ-
ing up notes in space as due to
weightlessness their pens
wouldn't write. They took this
up with Fishers their suppliers
who said they would see what
they could do.

After spending months and a
great deal of money on research
they came up with a suitable pen
that solved the problem.

Later on the Americans asked the
Russians if they'd had the same
problem.The answer was of course
YES. On being asked how they
overcame it the Russians replied
"We used pencils."
               - I liked that! -


I hope this is of some interest.
You provide us with an excellent
DISCZINE. I for one am very
grateful. Please don't stop.

           Sincerely

           Vic Bishop

Ron Cavers to Vic Bishop



I was interested to read about
this pen because, back in the
60's, I was bought a Fisher
Space Pen as a present. "It will
write upside down, under water
or in the weightlessness of
space" it was claimed. And it
did! (Well, I never tried going
into space - somehow, I could
never quite get the old Ford Pop
up to speed for take-off!).

The pen didn't rely on gravity
to feed the ink to the ballpoint
(as with normal pens); instead,
if I remember correctly, there
was a tiny cylinder of gas in


the end of the ink tube which
forced the ink to the point and
allowed you to write at any
angle without your words fading
away. Not quite sure why it
worked under water but it did.


It even came with a little widg-
et which allowed you to insert
the refills (which were quite
expensive)into a standard Parker
pen - although why you would
want to do this I don't know
because the Fisher pen itself
was very well crafted and comf-
ortable to hold. I would have
been happier to see some method
of using Parker refills in the
Fisher Pen. Ah well, it was a
long time ago...


What's that, you say? If it was
so good why am I not still using
it?...


Well, one day the gas cylinder
went bananas, flexed its muscles
and started forcing out ink at a
rapid rate of knots - I tried
writing as fast as I could to
keep up with it but to no avail,
I just couldn't keep up with
technology gone mad - just like
today.


Did they ever find the real rea-
son for the Apollo 13 disaster?
It couldn't have been an explod-
ing pen, could it?



            FOOTNOTE

Writing this prompted me to
search the cupboards and .. Yes,
here it is, still working after
all these years (surely a normal
pen would have dried out long
ago - it must be 30 years old).

Doesn't seem to be leaking...
I'll start using it again...
wonder if its worth anything...
must write to the Antiques
Roadshow and see when they are
in Leicester again.



                       Ron

From: Fred J. Ridout, SWINDON

Dear Ed's,

I have a couple of points that I
would like to put to you. The
first is I have a Basic program
called Notepad: one of my own in
which I use PFN fonts. I store
these in the RAMDISC on both my
+2/+D and +3 so that I only have
in the main program one font at
a time (gives me more memory in
the main program).

When loading up the RAMDISC on
the +3 I can use...

10 COPY "a:98?*"to"m:"

..and it will load all 20 fonts,
ie,from 9870 to 9890 lines,

But,on the +2/+D setup I have to
use...

10 LOAD D1"9870":SAVE !"9870"

   ...in blocks of ten as the +2
will only accept ten in one line
and I have to remove the line
number to run. This means that I
have to use two programs to
transfer all 20 fonts to the RAM
DISC.

What I would like to know is, is
there any method in Basic to
speed up this transfer on the +2
+D setup?

By the way, in case you may won-
der,each load comprises 19 blank
lines e.g, 9880: and one font:
9881 REM.

Secondly, could you let us know
if the BIG SIX program can be
altered to make a separate prog-
ram for the midweek national lo-
ttery numbers?

I hope all this makes some sort
of sense to you. I have been
altering this letter to try and
clarify it, I hope that I've
succeeded.

             Yours,


            F.J.Ridout

Brian Cavers to Fred Ridout

The only thing in your letter I
am not clear about is when you
say you save the PFN fonts in
'blocks of ten' on the +2/+D. Do
you mean you have only two font
files each containing ten fonts
and that you MERGE in each block
as needed?

I would have saved each font as
a separate file and chained them
thus...

  10 SAVE!"FONT1":LOAD D1"FONT2"
9881 REM FONT 1

The above would be saved on disk
with...
     SAVE "FONT1" LINE 10


With all twenty files saved in
that way they would all load in
order and save themselves to RAM
DISK and the final one would
load your main program. You can
then MERGE in each font as you
need it.As you have already got,
you need blank lines in each
font file to overwrite any font
already in memory.This seems too
obvious so I guess I have mis-
understood you. I don't really
understand why you saved them in
blocks of ten instead of separ-
ately. If this doesn't help, why
not send your full program and I
can then see exactly how you've
done it? You actually ask how to
speed up the transfer to RAMDISK
and I guess my method is slower.
but surely it only takes a few
seconds either way?

Regarding your BIG SIX question,
Ron, who wrote the program, says
that he can think of no quick
and easy solution. He will try
to study the program in detail
but, as ever, it is hard to find
time.

One thing you might consider is
to just regard the word 'WEEK'
in the program as 'DRAW' and use
it with 'DRAW No.' access only.
That is, the dates will all be
wrong but you should, at least,
be able to use it. It might be
worth a try.

                        Brian

From Brian Cavers, LEICESTER

This is a maths puzzle that may
interest some of you. If you saw
the BBC2 series THE NUMBERS GAME
recently then one of the prog-
rams was about Bayes Theorem. I
feel that the program presenter,
Fisher Dilke, is rather poor at
explaining things clearly so if
you were left in the dark about
the 'three-card trick' they used
as an example, here is my own
explanation. However, I did not
use Bayes Theorem but simple
logic.

Take three cards, one is red on
both sides, one is green on both
sides, and one is red on one
side and green on the other...


You can make up a set easily
with plain card or even paper
and just write R and G on the
relevant sides if you want to
experiment and have an aid to
your thought processes.

The three cards are shuffled
behind someone's back and not
only may the position of the
cards be shuffled, but any cards
may be rotated at random.

Finally, a card is pulled out at
random and presented face down
so you can only see one face.Let
us suppose the visible face is
red. The question to be asked is
what are the odds of the other
side also being red? WORK OUT
YOUR ANSWER NOW BEFORE PROCEED-
ING TO THE NEXT PAGE!...

Apparently most people would
give the answer 50%, ie, an even
chance of red or green.The reas-
oning goes something like this..

Since the top surface of the
card is red then it cannot be
the all-green card - it can only
be either the all-red card or
the red-green card so there is
an even chance of either. Or...

Because red and green are both
'represented' equally in the
cards then the chances of any
face being any particular colour
should also be evens.

Press 'F' to see the true answer
to the question...



The correct answer is 66.666% or
two chances out of three. In
other words you can safely bet
even money and over a period you
are bound to win two times out
of three!

The program presenter then gave
no sensible explanation for this
but merely quoted Bayes Theorem
in a way deliberately calculated
to impress as complicated rather
than to clarify. This is what I
did...

First I wrote a computer program
to simulate the cards and indeed
it did come up 66.6% (in fact it
hovered around 66.2% but I
assume I had some rounding up or
down error somewhere).


Having satisfied myself that the
answer given was true I reasoned
it out thus...

The 'deception' seems to be in
the natural human reaction to
regard the red/red card as a
whole and consider it irrelevent
as to which way up it is - after
all it is still red on top and
red underneath whichever way it
is presented! However, for this
you need to consider FACES and
not cards...

There are SIX faces: three red
and three green. Let us call the
faces of the red/red card'RED 1'
and 'RED 2' and the red face of
the red/green card 'RED 3'. The
same can be done for the green..


When the cards are shuffled and
rotated and a card pulled out at
random, say, red on top,then the
visible side could be one of
THREE sides: RED 1, RED 2, RED 3
However, the chosen card's other
(hidden) side can only be RED 1,
RED 2 or GREEN 3. You can see at
once that there are two chances
of it being red: RED1 or RED 2
but only one chance of it being
green: GREEN 3.

Another way to  reason it is to
do the whole operation WITHOUT
the green/green card! This is
perfectly legitimate although it
means if green is turned up you
cannot continue with the test.
However, if red is presented it
is immediately obvious that...
.

There are three reds and only
one green if you don't have the
green/green card. One red is
already displayed so clearly
there are two other red sides
but only one green.

Well, once you grasp that it
seems obvious - a child could
see it - so why did the program
not clarify it that way?

If anyone can explain this by
actually using Bayes Theorem
then please write in! I assume
that perhaps the example used
was simple enough to grasp by
reason alone but more complex
situations might benefit from
the theorem.



Since writing this letter I saw
an 'episode' of 'PUT IT TO THE
TEST' with Carol Vorderman on
BBC1 with a very similar strange
mathematical phenomenon...


The scenario is a quiz show and
the contestant is offered to
pick one of three boxes: A, B or
C. Two contain a booby prize but
one has the star prize of the
keys to a brand new Porsche.

The contestant selects one box
and the compere then says "Let's
see what you WOULD have got if
you had opened...". The compere
then opens one of the boxes that
the contestant did NOT select,to
reveal one of the booby prizes.


The compere then says "would you
like to change your mind and
swap your selected box for the
other unopened box?"The audience
of course, shout out what they
think the contestant should do.

What would YOU do?

Think about it and then press F
for the next page to read the
amazing truth!...











Astonishly, the correct thing to
do is to SWAP your chosen box
for the other box and you then
have a better chance of winning
the star prize.Don't believe it?
Here's why...

Most people would 'feel' that it
is generally better in life to
be decisive and stick to your
decision.If you do but are wrong
then it would not 'feel' so bad
as changing your mind and THEN
being wrong because you would
'feel' you had actually got the
star prize in your grasp but
lost it! However, COMMON SENSE
says there is no difference at
all as there is obviously an
equal chance of either box con-
taining the star prize. WRONG!


When you first make your choice
from the three unopened boxes
you have TWO chances out of
three of being 'wrong'.Therefore
the odds are TWO TO ONE that you
have chosen a booby prize.

That being so, when the other
booby prize is revealed then the
odds are STILL two to one that
you have chosen a booby prize!

It follows that the star prize
will be in the remaining box
twice as often in that situation
as not. Your chances are there-
fore DOUBLED if you change your
mind! Weird or what?

                       Brian



From: Alan Sharvell, HARROW




Dear Brian and Ron,

Getting the latest (113) Outlet
reminded me that I intended to
write to you some time ago reg-
arding the problems which we are
going to experience with the
Channel 5 and our Spectrums. I
know that Brian Gaff gave a word
of warning regarding the dreaded
retuners which was something
that had done the rounds for
some time. It now appears that
there was something in it after
all as the time scale has now
been altered.


In the meantime, not being will-
ing to await the dreaded hour I
decided to abandon the TV as a
monitor and invest in an AMSTRAD
CTM 464 monitor which I picked
up for 35 quid including a 464 +
joysticks and games(since flogg-
ed on). The improvement in pict-
ure quality was amazing once I
had traced a suitable lead. I

would do providing you know the
outputs. Also you may like to
know that "ALCHEMIST SOFTWARE"
in Bristol have been working on

hear.

             Cheers

         Alan Sharvell

ict with other equipment and its

This is a maths puzzle that may interest some of you. If you saw the BBC2 series THE NUMBERS GAME recently then one of the prog- rams was about Bayes Theorem. I feel that the program presenter, Fisher Dilke, is rather poor at explaining things clearly so if you were left in the dark about the 'three-card trick' they used as an example, here is my own explanation. However, I did not use Bayes Theorem but simple logic.

Take three cards, one is red on both sides, one is green on both sides, and one is red on one side and green on the other...

You can make up a set easily with plain card or even paper and just write R and G on the relevant sides if you want to experiment and have an aid to your thought processes.

The three cards are shuffled behind someone's back and not only may the position of the cards be shuffled, but any cards may be rotated at random.

Finally, a card is pulled out at random and presented face down so you can only see one face.Let us suppose the visible face is red. The question to be asked is what are the odds of the other side also being red? WORK OUT YOUR ANSWER NOW BEFORE PROCEED- ING TO THE NEXT PAGE!...

Apparently most people would give the answer 50%, ie, an even chance of red or green.The reas- oning goes something like this..

Since the top surface of the card is red then it cannot be the all-green card - it can only be either the all-red card or the red-green card so there is an even chance of either. Or...

Because red and green are both 'represented' equally in the cards then the chances of any face being any particular colour should also be evens.

Press 'F' to see the true answer to the question...

The correct answer is 66.666% or two chances out of three. In other words you can safely bet even money and over a period you are bound to win two times out of three!

The program presenter then gave no sensible explanation for this but merely quoted Bayes Theorem in a way deliberately calculated to impress as complicated rather than to clarify. This is what I did...

First I wrote a computer program to simulate the cards and indeed it did come up 66.6% (in fact it hovered around 66.2% but I assume I had some rounding up or down error somewhere).

Having satisfied myself that the answer given was true I reasoned it out thus...

The 'deception' seems to be in the natural human reaction to regard the red/red card as a whole and consider it irrelevent as to which way up it is - after all it is still red on top and red underneath whichever way it is presented! However, for this you need to consider FACES and not cards...

There are SIX faces: three red and three green. Let us call the faces of the red/red card'RED 1' and 'RED 2' and the red face of the red/green card 'RED 3'. The same can be done for the green..

When the cards are shuffled and rotated and a card pulled out at random, say, red on top,then the visible side could be one of THREE sides: RED 1, RED 2, RED 3 However, the chosen card's other (hidden) side can only be RED 1, RED 2 or GREEN 3. You can see at once that there are two chances of it being red: RED1 or RED 2 but only one chance of it being green: GREEN 3.

Another way to  reason it is to do the whole operation WITHOUT the green/green card! This is perfectly legitimate although it means if green is turned up you cannot continue with the test. However, if red is presented it is immediately obvious that... .

There are three reds and only one green if you don't have the green/green card. One red is already displayed so clearly there are two other red sides but only one green.

Well, once you grasp that it seems obvious - a child could see it - so why did the program not clarify it that way?

If anyone can explain this by actually using Bayes Theorem then please write in! I assume that perhaps the example used was simple enough to grasp by reason alone but more complex situations might benefit from the theorem.

Since writing this letter I saw an 'episode' of 'PUT IT TO THE TEST' with Carol Vorderman on BBC1 with a very similar strange mathematical phenomenon...

The scenario is a quiz show and the contestant is offered to pick one of three boxes: A, B or C. Two contain a booby prize but one has the star prize of the keys to a brand new Porsche.

The contestant selects one box and the compere then says "Let's see what you WOULD have got if you had opened...". The compere then opens one of the boxes that the contestant did NOT select,to reveal one of the booby prizes.

The compere then says "would you like to change your mind and swap your selected box for the other unopened box?"The audience of course, shout out what they think the contestant should do.

What would YOU do?

Think about it and then press F for the next page to read the amazing truth!...

Astonishly, the correct thing to do is to SWAP your chosen box for the other box and you then have a better chance of winning the star prize.Don't believe it? Here's why...

Most people would 'feel' that it is generally better in life to be decisive and stick to your decision.If you do but are wrong then it would not 'feel' so bad as changing your mind and THEN being wrong because you would 'feel' you had actually got the star prize in your grasp but lost it! However, COMMON SENSE says there is no difference at all as there is obviously an equal chance of either box con- taining the star prize. WRONG!

When you first make your choice from the three unopened boxes you have TWO chances out of three of being 'wrong'.Therefore the odds are TWO TO ONE that you have chosen a booby prize.

That being so, when the other booby prize is revealed then the odds are STILL two to one that you have chosen a booby prize!

It follows that the star prize will be in the remaining box twice as often in that situation as not. Your chances are there- fore DOUBLED if you change your mind! Weird or what?

Brian

Ведущий передачи не дал этому никакого толкового объяснения, а лишь процитировал теорему Байеса — причём так, чтобы нарочно показаться сложным и умным, вместо того чтобы всё прояснить. И вот что сделал я...

Сначала я написал компьютерную программу для симуляции карточек, и она действительно выдала результат 66.6% (точнее, крутилась вокруг 66.2%, но, полагаю, у меня где-то закралась погрешность округления).

Убедившись, что данный ответ верен, я рассудил следующим образом...

«Подвох», судя по всему, кроется в естественной человеческой реакции воспринимать красно-красную карточку как единое целое и считать неважным, какой стороной вверх она лежит — ведь в любом случае сверху красный и снизу красный! Однако здесь нужно рассматривать СТОРОНЫ, а не карточки...

Всего есть ШЕСТЬ сторон: три красных и три зелёных. Назовём стороны красно-красной карточки «КРАСНАЯ 1» и «КРАСНАЯ 2», а красную сторону красно-зелёной карточки — «КРАСНАЯ 3». То же самое можно проделать и для зелёных...

Когда карточки перемешаны, перевёрнуты и одна вытащена наугад (скажем, сверху оказалась красная), видимая сторона может быть одной из ТРЁХ: КРАСНАЯ 1, КРАСНАЯ 2 или КРАСНАЯ 3. Однако другая (скрытая) сторона выбранной карточки может быть только КРАСНОЙ 1, КРАСНОЙ 2 или ЗЕЛЁНОЙ 3. Сразу видно, что есть два шанса на то, что она окажется красной (КРАСНАЯ 1 или КРАСНАЯ 2), и всего один шанс, что зелёной: ЗЕЛЁНАЯ 3.

Другой способ рассуждения — проделать всю операцию ВООБЩЕ БЕЗ зелёно-зелёной карточки! Это абсолютно законно, хотя и означает, что если выпадет зелёный, продолжать тест нельзя. Однако если показался красный, то сразу очевидно, что...

Без зелёно-зелёной карточки у нас есть три красных стороны и всего одна зелёная. Один красный уже показан, так что совершенно очевидно остаются две другие красные стороны и всего одна зелёная.

Что ж, стоит это уловить, как всё становится очевидным — даже ребёнок поймёт, так почему же в передаче не объяснили всё именно так?

Если кто-то может объяснить это, непосредственно применив теорему Байеса, пожалуйста, напишите! Полагаю, использованный пример был достаточно прост, чтобы понять его обычной логикой, но в более сложных ситуациях польза от теоремы, возможно, была бы заметнее.

Уже после написания этого письма я увидел выпуск передачи «PUT IT TO THE TEST» с Carol Vorderman на BBC1 с очень похожим странным математическим феноменом...

Сценарий викторины таков: участнику предлагают выбрать один из трёх ящиков: A, B или C. В двух из них лежит утешительный приз-пустышка, а в одном — суперприз: ключи от новенького Porsche.

Участник выбирает один ящик, после чего ведущий говорит: «Давайте посмотрим, что вы могли бы получить, если бы открыли...». Затем ведущий открывает один из ящиков, который участник НЕ выбирал, и показывает, что там пустышка.

После этого ведущий спрашивает: «Хотите ли вы изменить своё решение и поменять выбранный ящик на оставшийся закрытый?» Зрители в зале, конечно же, выкрикивают, как, по их мнению, должен поступить игрок.

А как поступили бы ВЫ?

Подумайте над этим, а затем нажмите F, чтобы перейти на следующую страницу и узнать поразительную правду!...

Как ни удивительно, правильное решение — ПОМЕНЯТЬ свой выбор на другой ящик, и тогда ваши шансы выиграть главный приз возрастут. Не верите? Вот почему...

Большинство людей нутром чувствуют, что в жизни вообще лучше проявлять решительность и стоять на своём. Если вы так поступите и ошибётесь, будет не так обидно, как если бы вы изменили решение и ТОЛЬКО ТОГДА проиграли — ведь покажется, что суперприз уже был у вас в руках, а вы его упустили! Однако ЗДРАВЫЙ СМЫСЛ подсказывает, что никакой разницы нет, ведь вероятность нахождения суперприза в любом из двух ящиков вроде бы одинакова. НЕВЕРНО!

Когда вы изначально делаете выбор из трёх закрытых ящиков, у вас ДВА шанса из трёх ошибиться. Следовательно, шансы того, что вы выбрали пустышку, составляют ДВА К ОДНОМУ.

Раз так, то когда открывается другая пустышка, вероятность того, что вы изначально выбрали пустышку, ВСЁ ЕЩЁ составляет два к одному!
